chapterTitle: Advanced CloudFront Configurations: Caching, Compression, and Security
aiGenerationNote: Create a 15-minute interactive lab walkthrough video. Begin by showing the CloudFront console. Guide the user through creating two custom cache policies: one for long-lived static content (high TTL, no query strings/headers/cookies in cache key, Brotli enabled) and one for short-lived API responses (low TTL, specific headers/query strings in cache key, no cookies). Then, demonstrate creating new cache behaviors in an existing distribution, associating them with specific path patterns (`/static/*`, `/api/*`) and the newly created cache policies. screens.title: Advanced CloudFront: Caching, Compression, and Security
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why advanced CloudFront configurations matter for global applications and how to apply them to reduce latency, cut origin costs, and harden your edge. We will move beyond the basics and focus on the control points CloudFront offers: Cache Policies and Origin Request Policies to shape cache behavior; TTL and cache key design that decide whether content is served from cache or your origin; automatic edge compression using Gzip and Brotli to reduce bandwidth; and AWS WAF and origin settings such as custom headers and timeouts to protect and verify requests. You will also see how Origin Shield can act as a regional cache to lower origin load, and how to use CloudWatch metrics and access logs to diagnose cache hit ratios and origin errors. Concrete examples include creating a long-lived policy for static assets, a short-lived policy for A P I responses, enabling Brotli compression for static files, and associating a WAF Web ACL to CloudFront. By the end, you should be able to decide what to include in a cache key, when to forward headers to your origin, and how to spot common misconfigurations that reduce cache effectiveness. Think about one asset your application serves often — how would you configure a cache policy for it so users get the fastest response while your origin stays calm?

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.3 › Overview
Advanced CloudFront: Caching, Compression, and Security
Fine-tune cache behavior, enable edge compression, and protect your origin with WAF and origin controls.
In this lesson

Learn cache and origin policies, TTLs and cache keys, Brotli/Gzip compression, WAF at the edge, origin headers and timeouts, Origin Shield, and monitoring with CloudWatch and logs.

Why it matters

Proper configuration means more cache hits, less origin load, faster page loads, and threats blocked before they reach your application.

Explore Key Topics
Cache Policies
Managed vs. custom policies control TTLs and cache-key parameters to improve hit ratio.
Compression
Enable Brotli and Gzip at the edge to reduce bytes transferred and speed up loads.
WAF & Origin Control
Filter threats at the edge and use custom headers and Origin Shield to protect and scale origins.
Interactive Concept Map
Cache Key
Select query strings, headers, cookies
Compression
Brotli preferred for static assets
WAF
Block common web exploits
Coming up: cache TTLs, cache key strategy, origin request policies, compression choices, WAF setup, origin verification, monitoring.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will master practical CloudFront configuration skills that matter in production. First, you will learn how to design and apply Cache Policies and Origin Request Policies to balance cache efficiency with correctness. For example, you will create a policy that caches static assets for long durations while forwarding only necessary headers to the origin. Second, you will implement edge compression using Gzip and Brotli to reduce payload sizes; you will learn when Brotli offers better results and why double compression must be avoided. Third, you will integrate AWS WAF with CloudFront to block common exploits at the edge and practice creating a Web ACL that starts in Count mode before switching to Block. Finally, you will configure advanced origin settings, such as custom headers for origin verification and connection or response timeouts, and learn to analyze CloudFront metrics and access logs to troubleshoot low cache hit ratios. Each objective links configuration decisions to measurable outcomes like cache hit ratio, origin load, and security posture so you can make informed trade-offs in production.

screens.title: Cache Policies: What they control
screens.narratorSegment: Cache Policies define how CloudFront caches content at edge locations. At their core a cache policy specifies TTL settings — Minimum, Default, and Maximum — and which request elements form the cache key, such as selected headers, query strings, and cookies. The Default TTL is used when the origin does not set cache-control headers. Minimum TTL can force short-lived origin headers to be ignored, ensuring a minimum caching period, while Maximum TTL caps how long objects can live even if the origin sets a very long expiry. A clear example is static image assets: you might create a policy with a high Default TTL and no headers, cookies, or query strings included in the cache key so many viewers hit the same cached object. Conversely, dynamic A P I responses need short TTLs and selective cache keys to avoid serving stale or incorrect data. A common misconception is that more parameters in the cache key always increase correctness. In fact, including unique session IDs or user-specific cookies will create unique cache entries per user and destroy hit ratios. To design a policy, identify which request attributes actually change the response and include only those. Key takeaway: a good cache policy balances correctness and reuse — include what matters, exclude what fragments the cache.

keyIdea.text: Include only request attributes that affect the response in the cache key, and set TTLs to match content freshness needs.

content.html:
Core Concept › Cache Policies
What a cache policy controls
TTL settings and cache key composition determine when CloudFront serves from cache or forwards to the origin.
  • Default TTL: used when origin does not send caching headers.
  • Minimum TTL: forces a lower bound on caching duration.
  • Maximum TTL: prevents overly long caching despite origin headers.
  • Cache key: which headers, query strings, and cookies are used to form the key.
Explanation bullets
  • Only identical cache keys map to the same cached object; mismatched keys cause misses.
  • Choose minimal query strings/headers in the key to improve hit ratio for static assets.
  • Use short TTLs for dynamic responses and longer TTLs for static assets like images or CSS.
Concrete example
Create a policy named LongLivedStaticAssetsPolicy with Minimum TTL 86400, Default TTL 2592000, Maximum TTL 31536000 and no headers, cookies, or query strings in the cache key. This groups identical static asset requests into a single cache entry across viewers.
Misconception check: Including user cookies like a session ID improves correctness — false. It fragments cache entries per user and reduces reuse.
Key Takeaway

Design cache policies by asking: which request attributes change the response? Include those only, and choose TTLs that match content volatility.

screens.title: TTL Settings: Minimum, Default, Maximum
screens.narratorSegment: TTLs are the primary mechanism that defines how long objects remain in CloudFront caches. Think of TTLs as three brakes on object lifetime. The Minimum TTL ensures objects are cached for at least a baseline period even if the origin advertises shorter caching. This can protect you from excessive origin load in noisy conditions. The Default TTL is used when the origin sends no explicit caching instructions — it acts as the fallback lifetime. The Maximum TTL caps object lifetime even if the origin asks for a very long expiry, preventing stale content from remaining indefinitely after unexpected origin changes. A typical configuration for static assets uses a high Default and Maximum TTL and a Minimum TTL of zero or a small value; for dynamic APIs, you set Minimum and Default to zero and a small Maximum. Concrete example: static assets may use Default TTL 2592000 (30 days) and Maximum TTL 31536000 (1 year), while an A P I might use Default 300 and Maximum 300. A common misconception is that longer TTLs always equal better performance. Longer TTLs improve hit ratio but risk serving stale content after updates. The right choice depends on how often the content truly changes and whether you have a cache-busting strategy. Closing question: what TTLs would you choose for versioned static assets versus user-specific A P I responses?

content.html:
Process Flow › TTL Settings
Minimum TTL
Forces a lower bound on caching. Useful to absorb spikes even if origin sets short cache-control values.
Use case: protect origin from sudden repeated requests for the same asset during peak traffic.
Default TTL
Used when origin omits cache headers. Choose a safe default based on asset volatility.
Example: Default TTL 2592000 for static assets when origin is silent.
Maximum TTL
Caps how long objects may live even if origin sets a long expiry. Prevents long-lived stale content.
Example: Maximum TTL 31536000 for versioned static assets; shorter maximums for content that may be updated unexpectedly.
Key Takeaway

Decide TTLs based on true update frequency and whether you use cache-busting. Long TTLs increase reuse; short TTLs preserve freshness.

screens.title: Cache Key Design: What to include and why
screens.narratorSegment: The cache key is the unique identifier CloudFront uses to store and retrieve objects. When you include a request attribute in the cache key, CloudFront treats differing values as different objects. That makes correctness possible for responses that vary by that attribute, but it also fragments the cache and lowers the hit ratio. Consider three types of parameters: headers, query strings, and cookies. Headers are useful when the response truly varies by header, such as an Accept-Language header driving localized content. Query strings matter for requests where parameters change the resource, like a search query. Cookies should only be included when the cookie affects the response, for example a feature-flag cookie that toggles content. A concrete pitfall: including a session or authentication cookie in the cache key will cause nearly every request to miss the cache, sending traffic to your origin and increasing cost. Conversely, excluding an essential header, like an authorization header for a private A P I, risks serving wrong content. Good design follows this rule: include only attributes that change the response. Use analytics to confirm that a parameter is needed before adding it to the cache key. Closing takeaway: test changes and measure CacheHitRatio to see the impact of cache-key decisions.

keyIdea.title: Cache key rule
keyIdea.text: Only include request attributes that materially change the returned content; avoid adding unique per-user values.

content.html:
Comparison › Cache Key Design
Headers
Include when the response changes by header, for example localization headers. Avoid including broad headers that vary per client.
Query Strings
Include only query params that change resource content; ignore tracking parameters that create unnecessary variants.
Cookies
Only include cookies that affect content. Never include per-session cookies like session IDs or auth tokens in the cache key.
Concrete scenario
A site uses ?v= for cache busting. Exclude this parameter from the cache key for image assets if you serve versioned filenames; include it only if the parameter truly alters content.
Key Takeaway

Measure and include only the request parameters that produce different responses. Use logs and metrics to validate the effect on cache hit ratio.

screens.title: Origin Request Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Origin Request Policies control which parts of the viewer request are forwarded to your origin when CloudFront needs to fetch content. This is intentionally separate from the cache key because you may want to forward information to the origin for logging or processing while keeping the cache key minimal. For example, you might not include a viewer's User-Agent in the cache key, but you may forward it to the origin for analytics. Origin Request Policies let you specify headers, query strings, and cookies to forward on a cache miss, without fragmenting the cache. A concrete pattern: use a minimal cache key for static assets, but forward the User-Agent and an X-Forwarded-For header in the origin request policy to allow analytics and client detection at the origin when necessary. A common misconception is that everything you forward must be in the cache key. That is false; forwarding is about origin needs, while the cache key is about caching effectiveness. When designing policies, separate the requirements for cache correctness from the requirements for origin processing and logging. This separation helps you both maximize cache reuse and still provide your origin with the data it needs.

content.html:
Definition › Origin Request Policies
What they do
Specify which headers, query strings, and cookies CloudFront forwards to the origin on a cache miss.
  • Forward for logging or origin-side logic without changing cache key behavior.
  • Keep cache key minimal while giving origin necessary context.
  • Common forward: User-Agent, X-Forwarded-For, specific query args needed for origin routing.
Example scenario
Static assets: minimal cache key (no headers), but forward User-Agent and a custom header X-Client-Meta for server logging and analytics when CloudFront needs the origin.
Misconception check: forwarding many headers requires including them in the cache key — not necessarily; you can forward them separately to avoid cache fragmentation.
Key Takeaway

Use origin request policies to give the origin what it needs while keeping the cache key lean for better reuse.

screens.title: Compression: Gzip vs Brotli
screens.narratorSegment: Compression at the CloudFront edge reduces bytes sent to viewers and speeds up downloads. CloudFront supports Gzip and Brotli; Brotli often achieves better compression ratios on text-based assets like H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript. That means smaller transfers and faster perceived load times for users. Typically you enable automatic compression in cache behaviors and let CloudFront compress at the edge when the viewer’s Accept-Encoding header indicates support. A concrete example: enable Brotli and Gzip for a LongLivedStaticAssetsPolicy so images served as text wrappers, C S S, and JavaScript are compressed before delivery. Important caution: ensure your origin is not already compressing the same content in a way that leads to double compression, which is inefficient and can cause issues. For APIs that return small JSON responses, compression might be less beneficial or handled by the origin; consider disabling edge compression for those behaviors. A common misconception is that compression always reduces load. It reduces bandwidth but adds C P U work; however, when done at the edge, it offloads origin C P U and can improve end-to-end performance. Closing reflection: for your largest text asset, which compressor would you prefer and why?

keyIdea.title: Compression principle
keyIdea.text: Enable Brotli for text assets when viewers support it; avoid double compression and evaluate benefits for small API payloads.

content.html:
Comparison › Gzip vs Brotli
Gzip
Widely supported, lower CPU cost than some Brotli modes, still effective for many assets.
Brotli
Often better compression ratios for text assets, recommended when supported by viewers for static files.
Concrete guidance
Enable both Gzip and Brotli for static assets in cache behaviors. Validate viewer Accept-Encoding to ensure compatibility and check origin compression to avoid duplication.
Key Takeaway

Brotli typically gives smaller files for text assets; enable it at the edge but confirm your origin isn’t already performing the same compression.

screens.title: Enable Compression and Update Cache Behavior (CLI example)
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough explains the conceptual steps to enable compression via the AWS CLI. The real update sequence is: fetch the current distribution configuration and ETag, modify the DefaultCacheBehavior to set Compress to true (and to reference a CachePolicyId if using a custom policy), then update the distribution with the modified configuration and ETag. The chapter shows a shell-style sequence to get the distribution config and ETag, prepare a modified JSON, and call update-distribution with the modified config and ETag. An important concrete point is that you generally modify the existing structure rather than creating a new distribution config from scratch. A common misconception is that enabling compression is a single flag on the distribution; in practice you modify cache behaviors and, when using custom cache policies, ensure the cache policy allows Accept-Encoding handling for Brotli and Gzip. Example code is provided in the visual panel to illustrate the conceptual CLI steps; treat it as a pattern you adapt with your distribution ID and policy IDs. Takeaway: always fetch and edit the current config and use the ETag to ensure you do not overwrite concurrent changes.

keyIdea.text: Fetch distribution config and ETag, modify DefaultCacheBehavior.Compress and CachePolicyId, then update with the ETag to enable compression safely.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Enable Compression
Conceptual CLI sequence
# Get the distribution ETag and config
DISTRIBUTION_ID="E123ABCDEF4567"
ETAG=$(aws cloudfront get-distribution-config --id $DISTRIBUTION_ID --query 'ETag' --output text)

# Fetch current config (simplified representation)
CURRENT_CONFIG=$(aws cloudfront get-distribution-config --id $DISTRIBUTION_ID)

# Modify the JSON: set DefaultCacheBehavior.Compress = true
# and associate a CachePolicyId that enables Brotli/Gzip handling.

# Update distribution with modified config and ETag
# aws cloudfront update-distribution \
#   --id $DISTRIBUTION_ID \
#   --distribution-config file://modified-config.json \
#   --if-match $ETAG
Note: This is a conceptual pattern. In practice, use a JSON tool like jq to edit the distribution config safely and preserve fields not shown here.
Example caution
Always fetch and patch the existing config; using the ETag prevents race conditions. Enable compression on the behavior that serves static assets and ensure the cache policy enables Accept-Encoding flags if required.
Key Takeaway

Follow a fetch-modify-update pattern and validate the updated behavior in a staging distribution before applying to production.

screens.title: AWS WAF Integration with CloudFront
screens.narratorSegment: Attaching AWS WAF to a CloudFront distribution filters malicious traffic at the nearest edge location, preventing threats from consuming origin resources. WAF lets you create a Web ACL and combine managed rule groups, such as the common rules set and bot control, with custom rules like IP blacklists or rate-based rules. A recommended workflow is to add managed rule groups first in Count mode so you can observe false positives, then switch the action to Block once you are confident. For example, adding the AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet helps detect S Q L injection and cross-site scripting patterns. A practical misconception to avoid is thinking WAF alone solves all security needs; it is a layer in a defense-in-depth approach and should be combined with origin protections like Origin Access Control and secure application code. CloudFront with WAF reduces origin load by blocking malicious requests at the edge. When designing rules, focus on broad classes of threat first, then add targeted custom rules for application-specific patterns. Key operational tip: monitor WAF metrics and CloudWatch logs to iterate rules and reduce false positives before switching to blocking mode.

CloudFront with WAF reduces origin load by blocking malicious requests at the edge. When designing rules, focus on broad classes of threat first, then add targeted custom rules for application-specific patterns. Key operational tip: monitor WAF metrics and CloudWatch logs to iterate rules and reduce false positives before switching to blocking mode.

keyIdea.title: WAF at the edge
keyIdea.text: Use WAF Web ACLs to block common web exploits at CloudFront edge locations; test rules in Count mode before blocking.

content.html:
Architecture › WAF Integration
How WAF works with CloudFront

Attach a Web ACL to your CloudFront distribution in the Global scope. Rules evaluate requests at the Edge and take actions like Count, Allow, or Block before the request reaches your origin.

Managed Rules
Use AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet to catch common exploit patterns.
Custom Rules
Add IP blacklists, rate-based rules, or application-specific patterns.
Best practice: start with Count mode to measure potential false positives, then promote rules to Block once you confirmed expected traffic is unaffected.
Concrete example
Create a Global Web ACL named MyCloudFrontWAF, attach your distribution, add AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and BotControl, keep them in Count initially, and monitor CloudWatch metrics.
Misconception check
WAF is not a substitute for secure application code or origin access controls; it is an edge-layer filter that reduces origin exposure.

screens.title: Advanced Origin Settings: Headers and Timeouts
screens.narratorSegment: Advanced origin settings give you precise control over how CloudFront communicates with your origin. Custom headers are a simple but effective tool: add a header like X-CloudFront-Verify with a secret value to ensure the origin accepts only requests forwarded by CloudFront and not direct internet requests. This helps protect your origin from bypass. Connection and response timeouts determine how long CloudFront waits to establish a connection and to receive a response; tuning these avoids long-lived requests consuming edge resources while also preventing premature failures for slow backends. For example, increase timeouts for origins that need more processing time, or reduce them for origins that should fail fast. Origin Shield is another origin-side control: when enabled it places a Regional Edge Cache between CloudFront edge locations and your origin, reducing the number of direct origin requests if you have multiple distributions or high miss rates. A misconception is that custom headers alone fully secure an origin; they are part of a layered approach that should include Origin Access Control and bucket policies for S3 origins. Closing thought: use custom headers and Origin Shield to both verify and protect your origin while selecting reasonable timeouts that reflect backend behavior.

keyIdea.title: Origin controls
keyIdea.text: Use custom headers for verification, tune connection and response timeouts for reliability, and enable Origin Shield when many misses hit the origin.

content.html:
Definition › Advanced Origin Settings
Custom Headers
Add a header like X-CloudFront-Verify with a shared secret so the origin can verify requests originate from CloudFront.
Use Origin Access Control for S3 origins alongside headers for stronger protection.
Connection & Response Timeouts
Tune how long CloudFront waits to connect and to receive a response from the origin. Longer timeouts help slow backends; shorter timeouts fail fast and free edge resources.
Origin Shield
Enable Origin Shield to route origin requests through a Regional Edge Cache, reducing origin traffic for multiple distributions or high miss rates.
Key Takeaway

Combine custom headers for verification, tuned timeouts for reliability, and Origin Shield to minimize origin load when appropriate.

screens.title: CloudWatch Metrics and Access Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring CloudFront is essential to spot where caching or origin behavior is causing issues. CloudFront exposes metrics through CloudWatch such as Requests, BytesDownloaded, CacheHitRatio, and OriginErrorRate. CacheHitRatio is a primary health indicator: a low ratio for static assets often points to an overly fragmented cache key, too many forwarded query strings, or short TTLs. CloudFront access logs record every request with details like viewer IP, request method, URI, status code, and whether the request was a cache hit or miss. Use access logs to find patterns: repeated unique query parameters, per-request cookies, or a single bad client causing many misses. For troubleshooting, start with metrics to identify anomalies, then inspect access logs for root cause. A common mistake is assuming the origin headers are the only source of TTL decisions; cache policies and distribution behaviors can override origin headers. Practical example: if images show low hit ratio despite long-origin max-age headers, check that the cache policy isn't including query strings or cookies in the key. Closing question: which metric would you check first when origin load suddenly spikes? CloudWatch Metrics and Access Logs means use cloudwatch metrics to detect anomalies and cloudfront access logs to trace cache miss causes such as cache-key fragmentation or short ttls.. In practical terms, diagnose cache hit ratios, origin errors, and request patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Monitoring & Troubleshooting › Metrics and Logs
Key metrics to watch
  • CacheHitRatio — high is good; low suggests fragmentation or short TTLs.
  • Requests and BytesDownloaded — track traffic and bandwidth.
  • OriginErrorRate — indicates origin problems creating retries and failures.
Use CloudWatch alarms on sudden drops in CacheHitRatio or rises in OriginErrorRate so you can investigate promptly.
Access logs
Delivered to S3, logs include viewer IP, URI, status, and hit/miss flags. They are the definitive source for diagnosing why requests bypass the cache.
# Example log fields
# date time x-edge-location sc-bytes c-ip cs-method cs-uri-stem sc-status x-edge-result-type
Key Takeaway

Use metrics to detect issues, then analyze access logs to find the cache-key or TTL configuration that explains low hit ratios or origin strain.

screens.title: Activity: Create two cache policies and attach behaviors
screens.narratorSegment: This guided activity walks through the steps conceptually so you can perform them in the console or CLI. Start by creating two cache policies. Policy one, LongLivedStaticAssetsPolicy, is for static assets: set Minimum TTL 86400, Default TTL 2592000, Maximum TTL 31536000, and exclude headers, cookies, and query strings from the cache key. Enable Brotli and Gzip. Policy two, ShortLivedAPICachePolicy, is for A P I responses: set Minimum TTL 0, Default TTL 300, Maximum TTL 300, include the Authorization and Accept headers in the cache key if your A P I response varies by them, and forward query strings as required. Next, update your CloudFront distribution: create a behavior for /assets/* and associate it with LongLivedStaticAssetsPolicy and an appropriate Origin Request Policy, for example Managed-AllViewer if you need CORS support. Create another behavior for /api/v1/* with ShortLivedAPICachePolicy, HTTPS-only viewer policy, and an origin request policy that forwards necessary headers and query strings. Finally, create a Global WAF Web ACL, attach the distribution, add AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and AWSManagedRulesBotControlRuleSet in Count mode, and monitor traffic. Misconception to avoid: do not include user-session cookies in the static assets cache key. Reflection: after deploying, which metric will you inspect first to confirm your changes?

keyIdea.title: Activity outcome
keyIdea.text: Create two targeted cache policies, attach them to behaviors, and integrate WAF to protect the distribution while validating via metrics.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity › Create cache policies & WAF
Part 1: Create Cache Policies
  1. Create LongLivedStaticAssetsPolicy with Min 86400, Default 2592000, Max 31536000, no headers/cookies/query strings, enable Brotli/Gzip.
  2. Create ShortLivedAPICachePolicy with Min 0, Default 300, Max 300, include Authorization and Accept headers if response varies, include query strings as needed.
Tip: name policies clearly so you can reuse them across behaviors and distributions.
Part 2: Attach Behaviors & WAF
  1. Create behavior for /assets/* and attach LongLivedStaticAssetsPolicy and an appropriate origin request policy.
  2. Create behavior for /api/v1/* and attach ShortLivedAPICachePolicy; use HTTPS-only viewer policy.
  3. Create Global WAF Web ACL, add managed rule sets in Count mode, associate with distribution, then monitor and switch to Block when safe.
Misconception check: Do not forward or include per-session cookies in static asset cache keys.
Key Takeaway

Deploy targeted policies for different content types, attach behaviors with correct origin forwarding, and validate using CacheHitRatio and WAF logs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why advanced CloudFront configurations matter for global applications and how to apply them to reduce latency, cut origin costs, and harden your edge. We will move beyond the basics and focus on the control points CloudFront offers: Cache Policies and Origin Request Policies to shape cache behavior; TTL and cache key design that decide whether content is served from cache or your origin; automatic edge compression using Gzip and Brotli to reduce bandwidth; and AWS WAF and origin settings such as custom headers and timeouts to protect and verify requests. You will also see how Origin Shield can act as a regional cache to lower origin load, and how to use CloudWatch metrics and access logs to diagnose cache hit ratios and origin errors. Concrete examples include creating a long-lived policy for static assets, a short-lived policy for A P I responses, enabling Brotli compression for static files, and associating a WAF Web ACL to CloudFront. By the end, you should be able to decide what to include in a cache key, when to forward headers to your origin, and how to spot common misconfigurations that reduce cache effectiveness. Think about one asset your application serves often — how would you configure a cache policy for it so users get the fastest response while your origin stays calm?

By the end of this chapter you will master practical CloudFront configuration skills that matter in production. First, you will learn how to design and apply Cache Policies and Origin Request Policies to balance cache efficiency with correctness. For example, you will create a policy that caches static assets for long durations while forwarding only necessary headers to the origin. Second, you will implement edge compression using Gzip and Brotli to reduce payload sizes; you will learn when Brotli offers better results and why double compression must be avoided. Third, you will integrate AWS WAF with CloudFront to block common exploits at the edge and practice creating a Web ACL that starts in Count mode before switching to Block. Finally, you will configure advanced origin settings, such as custom headers for origin verification and connection or response timeouts, and learn to analyze CloudFront metrics and access logs to troubleshoot low cache hit ratios. Each objective links configuration decisions to measurable outcomes like cache hit ratio, origin load, and security posture so you can make informed trade-offs in production.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on outcomes and troubleshooting habits you will practice. You will create two concrete cache policies: one with long TTLs for static assets and one with short TTLs for dynamic A P I responses. You will practice enabling Brotli and Gzip in cache behaviors and learn how to check that your origin is not double-compressing content. You will configure a WAF Web ACL in the Global scope for CloudFront, attach managed rule groups, and iterate rules using Count mode before moving to Block. You will also set up origin controls: add custom headers for verification, tune connection and response timeouts, and enable Origin Shield for high-miss scenarios. Finally, you will read CloudWatch metrics like CacheHitRatio and OriginErrorRate and use CloudFront access logs to investigate patterns of cache misses. These skills help you move from configuration to operational confidence: when the cache hit ratio drops, you will know where to look and which policy parameters to adjust.

Cache Policies define how CloudFront caches content at edge locations. At their core a cache policy specifies TTL settings — Minimum, Default, and Maximum — and which request elements form the cache key, such as selected headers, query strings, and cookies. The Default TTL is used when the origin does not set cache-control headers. Minimum TTL can force short-lived origin headers to be ignored, ensuring a minimum caching period, while Maximum TTL caps how long objects can live even if the origin sets a very long expiry. A clear example is static image assets: you might create a policy with a high Default TTL and no headers, cookies, or query strings included in the cache key so many viewers hit the same cached object. Conversely, dynamic A P I responses need short TTLs and selective cache keys to avoid serving stale or incorrect data. A common misconception is that more parameters in the cache key always increase correctness. In fact, including unique session IDs or user-specific cookies will create unique cache entries per user and destroy hit ratios. To design a policy, identify which request attributes actually change the response and include only those. Key takeaway: a good cache policy balances correctness and reuse — include what matters, exclude what fragments the cache.

TTLs are the primary mechanism that defines how long objects remain in CloudFront caches. Think of TTLs as three brakes on object lifetime. The Minimum TTL ensures objects are cached for at least a baseline period even if the origin advertises shorter caching. This can protect you from excessive origin load in noisy conditions. The Default TTL is used when the origin sends no explicit caching instructions — it acts as the fallback lifetime. The Maximum TTL caps object lifetime even if the origin asks for a very long expiry, preventing stale content from remaining indefinitely after unexpected origin changes. A typical configuration for static assets uses a high Default and Maximum TTL and a Minimum TTL of zero or a small value; for dynamic APIs, you set Minimum and Default to zero and a small Maximum. Concrete example: static assets may use Default TTL 2592000 (30 days) and Maximum TTL 31536000 (1 year), while an A P I might use Default 300 and Maximum 300. A common misconception is that longer TTLs always equal better performance. Longer TTLs improve hit ratio but risk serving stale content after updates. The right choice depends on how often the content truly changes and whether you have a cache-busting strategy. Closing question: what TTLs would you choose for versioned static assets versus user-specific A P I responses?

The cache key is the unique identifier CloudFront uses to store and retrieve objects. When you include a request attribute in the cache key, CloudFront treats differing values as different objects. That makes correctness possible for responses that vary by that attribute, but it also fragments the cache and lowers the hit ratio. Consider three types of parameters: headers, query strings, and cookies. Headers are useful when the response truly varies by header, such as an Accept-Language header driving localized content. Query strings matter for requests where parameters change the resource, like a search query. Cookies should only be included when the cookie affects the response, for example a feature-flag cookie that toggles content. A concrete pitfall: including a session or authentication cookie in the cache key will cause nearly every request to miss the cache, sending traffic to your origin and increasing cost. Conversely, excluding an essential header, like an authorization header for a private A P I, risks serving wrong content. Good design follows this rule: include only attributes that change the response. Use analytics to confirm that a parameter is needed before adding it to the cache key. Closing takeaway: test changes and measure CacheHitRatio to see the impact of cache-key decisions.

Origin Request Policies control which parts of the viewer request are forwarded to your origin when CloudFront needs to fetch content. This is intentionally separate from the cache key because you may want to forward information to the origin for logging or processing while keeping the cache key minimal. For example, you might not include a viewer's User-Agent in the cache key, but you may forward it to the origin for analytics. Origin Request Policies let you specify headers, query strings, and cookies to forward on a cache miss, without fragmenting the cache. A concrete pattern: use a minimal cache key for static assets, but forward the User-Agent and an X-Forwarded-For header in the origin request policy to allow analytics and client detection at the origin when necessary. A common misconception is that everything you forward must be in the cache key. That is false; forwarding is about origin needs, while the cache key is about caching effectiveness. When designing policies, separate the requirements for cache correctness from the requirements for origin processing and logging. This separation helps you both maximize cache reuse and still provide your origin with the data it needs.

Compression at the CloudFront edge reduces bytes sent to viewers and speeds up downloads. CloudFront supports Gzip and Brotli; Brotli often achieves better compression ratios on text-based assets like H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript. That means smaller transfers and faster perceived load times for users. Typically you enable automatic compression in cache behaviors and let CloudFront compress at the edge when the viewer’s Accept-Encoding header indicates support. A concrete example: enable Brotli and Gzip for a LongLivedStaticAssetsPolicy so images served as text wrappers, C S S, and JavaScript are compressed before delivery. Important caution: ensure your origin is not already compressing the same content in a way that leads to double compression, which is inefficient and can cause issues. For APIs that return small JSON responses, compression might be less beneficial or handled by the origin; consider disabling edge compression for those behaviors. A common misconception is that compression always reduces load. It reduces bandwidth but adds C P U work; however, when done at the edge, it offloads origin C P U and can improve end-to-end performance. Closing reflection: for your largest text asset, which compressor would you prefer and why?

This walkthrough explains the conceptual steps to enable compression via the AWS CLI.
